title: Early Classes = Sleepy Teens
summary: Đọc về giấc ngủ của thanh thiếu niên và giờ bắt đầu học.
passage: A. Surveys of American teenagers find that about half of them do not get enough sleep on school nights. They get an average of sixty to ninety minutes less than experts say they need. One reason is biology. Experts say teens are programmed to go to sleep later and wake up later than other age groups. Yet many schools start classes as early as seven in the morning.

B. A clinical psychologist says teens need eight to ten hours of sleep a night. Sleepy teens can experience depression, and tired drivers can be dangerous. He says that starting classes later is one thing schools can do. Studies show that students can improve by a full letter grade in their first and second classes.

C. At St. George's School, the head teacher tried a thirty-minute delay. Visits to the health centre by tired students decreased by half. Late arrivals to first period fell by a third. Students said that they were less sleepy during the day, and teachers noticed a more positive mood.

title: Writing About Test Fears
summary: Đọc nghiên cứu về lo lắng trước kỳ thi và một can thiệp ngắn.

source.title: Anxious Students Gain on Tests by Writing About Fears

passage: A. Some students get so nervous before a test that they do poorly even when they know the material. Psychology professor Sian Beilock says that worrying about consequences uses attention and memory resources that could otherwise be used to focus on the exam.

B. Beilock and researcher Gerardo Ramirez developed a possible solution. Just before an exam, anxious students spent ten minutes writing about their worries. In a study, students who sat quietly performed an average of twelve percent worse on a second test. Students who wrote about their fears improved by an average of five percent.

C. The researchers also worked with younger students in a biology class. Before final exams, students either wrote about their feelings or thought about unrelated things. Highly anxious students who did the writing received an average grade of B+, compared with a B- for those who did not. The researchers say students can also try the technique at home or in a library.

title: Learning from Failure
summary: Đọc về cách tổ chức học hỏi từ thất bại và thay đổi quyết định.

source.title: How Failure Can Lead to Long-Lasting Knowledge

passage: A. A study says organizations learn more from failures than from successes, and keep that knowledge longer. Researchers Vinit Desai and Peter Madsen did not find much long-term organizational learning from success. They found that knowledge gained from failure can last for years.

B. The study looked at organizations that launch satellites and other space vehicles. In 2002, insulating material damaged a rocket on Atlantis, but the flight was considered a success. In 2003, insulation struck Columbia during launch. The shuttle broke apart on re-entry, seven crew members died, and NASA suspended flights while an investigation suggested changes.

C. Desai says searching for solutions after a failure can make leaders more open-minded. He points to airlines as an industry that has learned from failures. He advises organizations to look for useful information in small failures and failures they avoided, and to encourage the open sharing of information.

title: Science Websites for Children
summary: Đọc về các nền tảng trực tuyến giúp trẻ em khám phá khoa học.
passage: A. Millions of children use the Internet every day to explore the web, play games and research school projects. The Mad Science Group launched a science-based social network called Mad Science Kids Club. It was designed for children between six and fourteen and aimed to let them build an online community while exploring scientific discovery.

B. The club included groups such as a Counting Club for children who enjoy mathematics and Cosmic Adventures for those interested in space. One application allowed children to ask science questions that were published with answers from experts. The Science Zone offered experiments that children and parents could do at home.

C. The report also describes other sites. One explained science-related news in accessible language and added definitions of important words. Another offered guides for making toys from everyday materials and explained the scientific theories behind them. The report notes that such projects could provide many hours of exploration, although it had not tested every activity itself.
